new_statements.quote: The position of stress within a word is perhaps the most elusive aspect of Tasmanian phonology. We have the following source material: [a] Walker marks each vowel with either ¯ or ˘; these marks apparently indicate accent rather than quantity (see the comment in Roth 1899, p.l of Appendix). [b] Norman uses the same marks, probably in the same way. [c] Milligan says 'when a double consonant or two consonants stand together, the first carries the accent ...' [...] From these sources it appears that a disyllabic word is always stressed on the first syllable, whereas a trisyllabic word can be stressed on either first or second syllable. Our only general conclusion concerning stress in Tasmanian is thus: any syllable except the last can bear stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Pan-Tasmanian inference from 19th-century accent marks (Walker; Norman = the Port Sorell wordlist), Milligan's remark, Tindale's transcriptions and the Fanny Cochrane Smith / 1972 Crowley recordings: disyllables are stressed on the first syllable; trisyllables on the first or the second syllable with no recoverable conditioning; stress is never final. No fixed position can be established. Ritz 1909 (pp. 48-49, also pan-Tasmanian, using the Norman vocabulary's parkallar 'bullock' as his example) reads the same marks differently: the accent 'was quite frequently on the third syllable from the end - the antepenult' and may have varied freely between speakers.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Crowley & Dixon. Taylor 2006 (MA thesis, pp. 160, 257-259) reads the bar/breve marks of Sterling ('Norman'), Robinson and Walker as regular strong initial stress with at most secondary stressing of later elements.
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the free first/second placement in trisyllables; Ritz 1909 p. 49 cites 'foot/leg' recorded with the accent on different syllables by different recorders as evidence of speaker-to-speaker variation.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress inferred from isolated citation forms in 19th-century wordlists (accent diacritics) and from later song/speech recordings; the statement is made for 'Tasmanian' as a whole, with Crowley & Dixon noting (p. 407) that their phonology rests mainly on the mid-eastern and south-eastern languages. No Port-Sorell-specific stress statement exists in any opened source; the Norman vocabulary (Curr 1887 vol. III pp. 611-616, the only wordlist Glottolog attaches to port1278) carries the marks but no accent note.
new_statements.identity_note: Port Sorell (port1278, xpl) is one of Crowley & Dixon's eight Tasmanian languages (their language (e), p. 403), known from Robinson-assigned items and from Norman's vocabulary (Curr 1887 vol. III pp. 611-616), which is the only wordlist Glottolog attaches to the code. The quoted stress statement is made for 'Tasmanian' as a whole (bookkeeping node tasm1247; the same statement serves brun1235, nort3415, benl1235 etc.), but it explicitly counts Norman's marked vocabulary as source [b]. Provenance of that vocabulary is disputed: Curr says only that it was collected at Port Sorell and that the tribes are unknown; Plomley 1976 (via Taylor 2006 p. 99) attributes it to Charles Sterling, Robinson's clerk, with mostly (south-)eastern words; its 'Names of natives' section is headed 'Ben Lomond Mob' (Curr p. 617); Bowern 2012 says it 'appears to group with the northeast languages'. So the wordlist behind port1278 may not be Port Sorell (western) speech at all. Language extinct since the 19th century; no speaker-based or instrumental description can exist.

readall_conflicts: The pre-existing conflict stands as recorded in our earlier reading: Crowley & Dixon 1981 sect. 2.4 (p. 413) give a pan-Tasmanian statement (disyllables initial, trisyllables first or second, never final, called 'the most elusive aspect of Tasmanian phonology'), while Ritz 1909 pp. 48-49 says the accent fell 'quite frequently on the third syllable from the end' and may have been free; neither is about Port Sorell specifically. The ESM adds an identity conflict rather than a stress conflict: it removes the Norman vocabulary from Port Sorell (Sterling, recorded at Sorell in the east; northeastern cluster) and identifies the Port Sorell list as Charles Robinson's NW-ps vocabulary, which carries no published stress remark.
